Notes: Earliest documented presence: Natronai Gaon wrote in 853 that Alisana (Lucena) was 'a Jewish place with no gentiles at all'; entirely Jewish city under Muslim rule; no count
First mention in an 853 responsum describing Lucena (Alisana) as 'a city of many Jews' with 'no Gentile in its midst'; no count
Hebrew Wikipedia: first mention in a responsum of 853 as a city of many Jews and a place with no gentiles; no count
Mid-9th century (midpoint 850 used): Amram Gaon sent his prayer book in response to a question by a scholar of Lucena; documented community, no count
Documentary data from late 9th century; 'Ciudad de los Judíos' 9th-12th c.; walled medina controlled exclusively by Jewish population; year = midpoint of 9th century
10th century (midpoint 950 used): Lucena's Jewry competed in importance with Córdoba's; some cemetery gravestones tentatively dated 9th-10th c.; no count

Jewish necropolis (discovered 2006) of at least 346 catalogued graves (a burial count over centuries, not a population); remains dated 1000-1050 (midpoint 1025 used); oldest Hebrew gravestone possibly 8th c.
11th century (midpoint 1050): yeshivah of Lucena with Isaac ibn Ghayyat, then Isaac Alfasi and Joseph ibn Migash; c.1090 Almoravid conversion demand, community saved by heavy bribe; many moved north
In 1066 the widow of Joseph b. Samuel ha-Nagid and son Azariah among refugees from Granada who came to Lucena; many Jews of Lucena later moved to Navarre near Tudela
Pact sealed in 1103 between Yusuf ibn Tashfin and the za'im (chief) of Lucena; Jewish city, no count
Yusuf ibn Teshufin went to Lucena (1107) to compel conversion; community negotiated payment; Jews 'richer than those of any other city'; rabbi elected by community acted as judge; no count
Academy of Lucena ended abruptly in 1145 when the Almohads arrived
Flourishing city 'the seat of Jewish science' destroyed by the Almohads (1146); no count
In 1146 during the Almohad wars Jews were persecuted, many forced to convert to Islam; 'The community ... totally disappeared.' Zero reflects source statement of total disappearance
Almohad conquest 1148: Jews 'drastically decreased in number', fled north; academy relocated to Toledo; Lucena 'effectively ceased to exist' as a Jewish centre (decline, not stated as zero)
In 1148 the city of the Jews was invaded and razed by the Almohads after Jews refused to convert to Islam; survivors went north to Toledo
Lucena conquered by Castile 1240; its Jewish community (Christian period) suffered 'total destruction' in the 1391 riots; no count
Spanish Wikipedia states that in 1492 the expulsion of the Jews took place, 'que constituía el mayor grupo demográfico de la localidad' (ambiguous wording; no count)
